item.mechanism: Directional solidification eliminates grain boundaries inclined at 45° to the loading direction, thereby removing shear stress pathways along weak boundaries and defining strength solely by the microstructure within longitudinal grains.
item.system: Base alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (directionally solidified vs. conventionally cast)
item.operating_conditions: Tensile testing from room temperature to 900 °C; annealing at 900 °C for 50 h; loading parallel to [001]-grain orientation
item.supporting_observation: Directional solidification samples showed a 1.5–1.8 factor increase in UTS at room temperature to 700 °C compared to conventionally cast samples, with reduced scatter in UTS and strain to failure.
item.scope_limits: The improvement factor drops to 1.1 at 800 °C and 1.0 at 900 °C, indicating the mechanism's benefit diminishes at higher temperatures.
item.alternatives_considered: Conventional casting with randomly oriented grains which exhibits grain boundaries across the orientation of external stress.
quotes: Avoiding grain boundaries inclined at 45° by the loading direction, shear stresses along these weaker boundaries can be eliminated
DS-samples scattered much less, as standard deviation of particularly ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and also strain to failure (ε f ) were reduced strongly
the most important improvement was the increase of UTS in case of the DS-samples by a factor of 1.5–1.8 in the range of room temperature up to 700 °C

item.mechanism: Molybdenum partitions to the matrix, causing solid-solution strengthening due to its larger atomic size which distorts the lattice and acts as an obstacle for dislocation movement.
item.system: Base alloy with 1.0 at.% Mo addition (Al 9 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 Mo 1)
item.operating_conditions: High-temperature tensile testing; annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h
item.supporting_observation: The Mo-alloy exhibited round γ′-particles and lower ultimate tensile strength compared to the base alloy and Hf-alloy under the same conditions.
item.scope_limits: The text notes that round γ′-particles contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior, and the Mo-alloy showed the worst behavior among DS samples between 600 and 800 °C.
item.alternatives_considered: Hafnium addition which sharpens γ′-corners and reduces Heusler phase content.
quotes: Molybdenum is supposed to partition to the matrix, to have a solid-solution strengthening effect due to its bigger atomic size and therefore to lead to a distorted lattice
Addition of 1 at.% molybdenum lead to round γ′-particles, while the Heusler type phase remained in its needle-like shape
Under the same heat treatment conditions, Mo addition lowered the ultimate tensile strength of the base alloy due to the more round morphology of γ′-particles

item.mechanism: Hafnium strengthens grain boundaries by participating in the γ′-phase (Ni3(Al, Hf)), creating a fracture-retarding interlocking configuration that enhances creep ductility and lifetime.
item.system: Base alloy with 0.5 at.% Hf addition (Al 9.5 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 Hf 0.5)
item.operating_conditions: High-temperature tensile testing; annealing at 950 °C/100 h
item.supporting_observation: The Hf-containing alloy showed the best mechanical properties among DS samples, with high reproducibility and increased UTS compared to the base alloy.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism relies on the specific formation of a spherical Heusler type phase and low content (<3%) for optimal results; the text states the Hf-alloy showed an increase in UTS due to lower content of Heusler phase.
item.alternatives_considered: Base alloy without Hf which has a higher volume fraction of Heusler type phase (9% vs 3-5%) and needle-like Heusler morphology.
quotes: The positive effect of hafnium is due to a strengthening of grain boundaries: A columnar-grained microstructure for example shows an enhancement of creep ductility and lifetime by the addition of hafnium that strengthens the vicinity of grain boundaries vertical to the load stress
The Hf-containing alloy, however, showed an increase in UTS due to the lower content and/or the spherical shape of Heusler type phase

item.mechanism: A low volume fraction of Heusler type phase (reduced from 9% to 3%) combined with cuboidal γ′-precipitates leads to high ultimate tensile strength, good strain to failure, and high reproducibility.
item.system: Base alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 annealed at 900 °C for 50 h
item.operating_conditions: Tensile testing from room temperature to 900 °C; annealing at 900 °C/50 h
item.supporting_observation: Samples annealed at 900 °C/50 h exhibited higher UTS and strain to failure with less scatter compared to those annealed at 950 °C/100 h where Heusler phase content increased.
item.scope_limits: If the Heusler type phase content rises three times higher (e.g., to 9%), the ultimate tensile strength falls down drastically.
item.alternatives_considered: Annealing at 950 °C/100 h which increases Heusler phase volume fraction to 9% and results in brittle fracture behavior.
quotes: The reason for this desirable behavior was due to the volume content of Heusler type phase that was drastically reduced from 9% to 3% after annealing at 900 °C/50 h
If the Heusler type phase content rose three times higher in the case of the base alloy, the ultimate tensile strength fell down drastically
The annealing treatment of 900 °C/50 h for the base alloy lead to a similar mechanical behavior to that of the Hf-containing alloy, with high strength, good strain to failure and high reproducibility

item.mechanism: Cuboidal γ′-precipitates with sharp corners provide better mechanical properties than round or cuboidal particles with rounded corners, assuming the Heusler type phase content is kept low.
item.system: Base alloy (900 °C/50 h) and Hf-alloy (950 °C/100 h) compared to Mo-alloy (950 °C/100 h)
item.operating_conditions: Tensile testing; annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h
item.supporting_observation: The Hf-alloy with sharp-cornered cubic precipitates and the base alloy (900 °C/50 h) with cuboidal precipitates showed the best properties, while the Mo-alloy with round particles showed the worst.
item.scope_limits: The mechanism is conditional on the Heusler phase content being low; the text states good properties occurred 'assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low'.
item.alternatives_considered: Round γ′-particles found in the Mo-alloy which contributed in a bad way to the mechanical behavior.
quotes: Consequently, good high-temperature tensile properties occurred in the case of cubic precipitates, assumed that the Heusler type phase content was kept quite low
While the base alloy showed cuboidal particles with rounded corners, the Mo-alloy exhibited spherical, and the Hf-alloy showed cubic, sharp-cornered precipitates

As the two strongest materials, the base alloy (900 °C/50 h) and the Hf-containing alloy (950 °C/100 h) exhibited almost identical stress–strain diagrams concerning strength, ductility and reproducibility

item.mechanism: The presence of a needle-like Heusler type phase with high volume fraction (9%) degrades mechanical properties, whereas a spherical shape with low content (<3%) is desirable.
item.system: Base alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (comparing 900 °C/50 h vs 950 °C/100 h treatments)
item.operating_conditions: Tensile testing; annealing at 900 °C/50 h (3% Heusler) vs 950 °C/100 h (9% Heusler)
item.supporting_observation: Samples with 9% Heusler phase showed brittle fracture and scattered stress-strain curves, while those with 3% Heusler phase showed high ductility and strength.
item.scope_limits: The text does not fully clarify the thermodynamic stability or exact chemical role of the Heusler phase, stating it is a 'top priority for future work'.
item.alternatives_considered: Avoiding the Heusler phase entirely to achieve a two-phase microstructure.
quotes: The top priority for future work is to reduce or maybe even avoid the Heusler type phase and to clarify the question about its role on mechanical behavior
We can state that a spherical shape and a low content of <3% is desirable for good mechanical properties
The Heusler type phase is very rich in Al, while all other elements are depleted, especially Fe, Co and Cr

item.mechanism: L1 2 -ordered, coherently embedded γ′-precipitates in an fcc-matrix provide particle strengthening similar to nickel-based superalloys, leading to high strength at room and high temperatures.
item.system: Base alloy Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6
item.operating_conditions: Annealing at 900 °C/50 h and 950 °C/100 h; tensile testing up to 900 °C
item.supporting_observation: The alloy exhibits L1 2 -ordered, coherently embedded precipitates in a fcc-matrix, comparable to nickel-based superalloys, with UTS exceeding commercial alloys like IN 617 and Alloy 800 H in the 700–800 °C range.
item.scope_limits: The strengthening effect is sensitive to precipitate morphology (cuboidal vs round) and the presence of the Heusler phase.
item.alternatives_considered: Single-phase solid-solution alloys which were not the focus; the authors note most alloys form intermetallic compounds.
quotes: This alloy composition is the base alloy for this work, exhibiting L1 2 -ordered, coherently embedded precipitates in a fcc-matrix, comparable to nickel-based superalloys
The cuboidal nanoscale particles lead to high strength at room and high temperatures
In the important temperature range between 700 and 800 °C, UTS of the base alloy was equal in the beginning and even exceeded IN 617 at 800 °C by a factor of 1.2

item.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single solid-solution phase if no intermetallic phase with low enthalpy of formation exists, but in this alloy system, intermetallic compounds form instead.
item.system: General High Entropy Alloy (HEA) theory applied to the Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti system
item.supporting_observation: The text contrasts the expected single-phase behavior with the actual formation of a three-phase microstructure (fcc matrix, L1 2 precipitates, Heusler phase).
item.scope_limits: The mechanism of single-phase stabilization does not hold for this specific composition; the authors note 'Most alloys containing at least five elements... do not crystallize as a single-phase solid-solution'.
item.alternatives_considered: Single-phase HEA design which was abandoned for the CCA approach in this work.
quotes: High configurational entropy, due to the large number of elements and similar concentrations, leads to a decrease in the Gibbs free energy and thus a stabilization of one solid-solution phase if no intermetallic phase with low enthalpy of formation exists
Most alloys containing at least five elements in near equiatomic composition, however, do not crystallize as a single-phase solid-solution, but rather form intermetallic compounds as secondary phases
Recognizing the difficulties of avoiding phase separation, a transition was made from developing a HEA to optimizing a CCA
